title: Nancy Kassebaum Baker, first woman elected to Senate without spouse's seat, dies at 94
dek: Nancy Kassebaum Baker, the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without a spouse already serving in Congress, died Friday at age 94 of natural causes. She served three terms representing Kansas from 1978 to 1997.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Per Fox News reporting, Nancy Kassebaum Baker, the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without a husband in Congress, died Friday at age 94 of natural causes.
bottom_line: Kassebaum Baker's career spanned a pivotal era of women's entry into high office and her death removes one of the most visible voices of Republican moderation from the political landscape. Her legacy now rests entirely in historical record and in the shape of the institutions and laws she influenced during her 18 years in the Senate.
body: Nancy Kassebaum Baker, the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without a spouse already serving in Congress, died Friday at age 94 of natural causes, her son Bill Kassebaum said, per Fox News reporting.

Kassebaum Baker won election to the Senate in 1978 and served three terms representing Kansas, retiring in 1997 after 18 years in office, according to Fox News. She was the daughter of Alf Landon, a former Kansas governor and the Republican Party's unsuccessful 1936 presidential nominee. By the time she announced her retirement, Fox News reports she was one of eight women serving in the Senate and the only woman chairing a Senate committee.

During her Senate career, Kassebaum Baker built a record as an independent-minded moderate. She supported an assault weapons ban backed by President Bill Clinton, a vote that generated the angriest mail of her Senate career, according to Fox News. In 1996, a landmark health insurance law bore her name alongside that of Democratic Massachusetts Senator Ted Kennedy. Kassebaum Baker won re-election with 76 percent of the vote in 1984 and 74 percent in 1990, per Fox News.

She married former Republican Senator Howard Baker of Tennessee in 1996, shortly before leaving the Senate, marking the first marriage between a man and woman who had both served in the Senate, Fox News reports. Howard Baker served as President Ronald Reagan's chief of staff and later as U.S. ambassador to Japan under President George W. Bush before his death in 2014.

After leaving Congress, Kassebaum Baker continued public service, serving on a bipartisan commission on campaign finance reform during the Clinton administration, according to Fox News. In later years, she increasingly broke with the Republican Party's direction and endorsed Democrats in several Kansas races, including Democratic Governor Laura Kelly. Following the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, she called for President Donald Trump's impeachment, telling Kansas City's KMBC that "This just has gone too far," per Fox News reporting.
